unsupported_claims: Graph factorization is applicable only to graphs of moderate size because it requires forming and factorizing an n-by-n matrix, which is costly in time and memory (the evidence says it uses SGD and scales to large graphs).
Graph factorization is transductive and cannot embed unseen nodes.
Graph factorization captures higher-order structure only if the matrix is explicitly constructed with it, e.g. via powers of the adjacency matrix.
Graph factorization is limited to homogeneous, single-relation networks.
LINE is applicable to a broader range of graph sizes than graph factorization, and graph factorization is more computationally demanding.
rationale: The core claim is supported: graph factorization applies only to undirected graphs, while LINE handles both undirected and directed graphs. The answer adds unsupported claims, including that graph factorization is limited to moderate-sized graphs, which contradicts the evidence that it is optimized with SGD and scales to large graphs; it also adds claims about transductivity and homogeneity.
